title: Chapter 18
paragraphs: After the conversation with Alexey Alexandrovitch, Vronsky stepped out onto the porch of the Karenins' house and stood there, struggling to remember where he was and where he was supposed to walk or drive. He felt disgraced, humiliated, guilty, and stripped of any possibility of washing the humiliation away. He felt knocked off the well-worn track along which he had so proudly and lightly walked until now. All the habits and rules of his life that had seemed so solid had turned out, all at once, to be false and useless. The betrayed husband, who up to that point had figured as a pitiful creature, an incidental and slightly ridiculous obstacle to his happiness, had suddenly been summoned by Anna herself and lifted to an awe-inspiring height — and from that height the husband had revealed himself, not as malicious, not as false, not as ridiculous, but as kind and straightforward and large. Vronsky couldn't help feeling this, and the roles had abruptly been reversed. He felt the other man's elevation and his own abasement, the other man's truth and his own falsehood. He felt that the husband was magnanimous even in his sorrow, while he had been base and petty in his deceit. But this sense of his own humiliation in front of the man he had unjustly looked down on was only a small part of his misery. He felt unutterably wretched now, because his passion for Anna, which had seemed to him lately to be cooling, was — now that he knew he had lost her forever — stronger than it had ever been. He had seen the whole of her in her illness, had come to know her very soul, and it seemed to him that he had never loved her till then. And now, when he had learned to know her, to love her the way she should be loved, he had been humiliated before her and had lost her forever, leaving her with nothing of himself but a shameful memory. Worst of all was his ridiculous, shameful position when Alexey Alexandrovitch had pulled his hands away from his humiliated face. He stood on the steps of the Karenins' house as though out of his mind, with no idea what to do.

Once home, after three sleepless nights, Vronsky lay down on the sofa without undressing, clasping his hands and resting his head on them. His head was heavy. Images, memories, ideas of the strangest sort followed each other in his mind with extraordinary speed and clarity. First it was the medicine he had poured out for the patient and spilled over the spoon, then the midwife's white hands, then the strange posture of Alexey Alexandrovitch on the floor beside the bed.

"Sleep! Forget!" he told himself with the calm confidence of a healthy man that if he's tired and sleepy, he'll fall asleep at once. And just then his head did begin to grow drowsy and he began to slip into oblivion. The waves of the sea of unconsciousness had begun to close over his head when — all at once — it felt as though a violent electric shock had passed through him. He started so violently that he leapt up on the springs of the sofa, and bracing himself on his arms, found himself in a panic on his knees. His eyes were wide open, as if he had never been asleep at all. The heaviness in his head and the weariness in his limbs that he had felt a minute before were suddenly gone.

"You can trample me in the mud," he heard Alexey Alexandrovitch saying, and saw him standing in front of him, and saw Anna's face with its burning flush and glittering eyes, gazing with love and tenderness not at him but at Alexey Alexandrovitch; he saw his own — as he imagined it — foolish, ridiculous figure when Alexey Alexandrovitch took his hands away from his face. He stretched out his legs again and threw himself onto the sofa in the same position and shut his eyes.
"Sleep! Forget!" he repeated to himself. But with his eyes closed he saw, more vividly than before, Anna's face as it had been on the memorable evening before the races.

"That isn't and won't be, and she wants to wipe it out of her memory. But I can't live without it. How can we be reconciled? How can we be reconciled?" he said aloud, and without realizing it began repeating the words. The repetition held back the rising tide of fresh images and memories that he could feel crowding into his brain. But the repeating of words didn't hold his imagination back for long. Again, in extraordinarily rapid succession, his best moments rose up before his mind, then his recent humiliation. "Take his hands away," Anna's voice says. He takes them away and feels the shame-struck, idiotic expression of his face.

He went on lying there, trying to sleep, though he knew there wasn't the slightest hope of it, and kept repeating stray words from some chain of thought, trying that way to hold off the rising flood of new images. He listened, and heard, in a strange, mad whisper, the words repeated: "I didn't value it, didn't make enough of it. I didn't value it, didn't make enough of it."

"What is this? Am I losing my mind?" he said to himself. "Maybe. What is it that makes people lose their minds; what makes them shoot themselves?" he answered himself, and opening his eyes, he saw, to his surprise, an embroidered cushion beside him, made by Varya, his brother's wife. He fingered the tassel of the cushion and tried to think of Varya, of when he had last seen her. But thinking of anything outside himself was an agonizing effort. "No, I have to sleep!" He pulled the cushion up and pressed his head into it, but it took an effort to keep his eyes shut. He jumped up and sat down. "That's all finished for me," he told himself. "I have to think what to do. What is left?" His mind ran rapidly over the parts of his life apart from his love for Anna.

"Ambition? Serpuhovskoy? Society? The court?" He couldn't get any of them to hold his attention. All of it had meant something before, but now there was no reality in any of it. He got up from the sofa, took off his coat, undid his belt, and, uncovering his hairy chest to breathe more easily, paced up and down the room. "This is how people go mad," he repeated, "and how they shoot themselves... to escape humiliation," he added slowly.

He went to the door and shut it, then with fixed eyes and clenched teeth he walked over to the table, picked up a revolver, looked around him, turned it to a loaded barrel, and sank into thought. For two minutes, his head bent forward in an expression of intense concentration, he stood with the revolver in his hand, motionless, thinking.

"Of course," he said to himself, as if a logical, continuous, clear chain of reasoning had brought him to an indisputable conclusion. In fact this "of course," which seemed so convincing to him, was simply the result of going around again through exactly the same circle of memories and images that he had already passed through ten times in the last hour — memories of happiness lost forever. There was the same conception of the meaninglessness of everything still to come in life, the same awareness of humiliation. Even the sequence of these images and emotions was the same.

"Of course," he repeated, when for the third time his thought passed around the same spellbound circle of memories and images, and pulling the revolver to the left side of his chest, gripping it firmly with his whole hand, as if squeezing it in his fist, he pulled the trigger. He didn't hear the sound of the shot, but a violent blow to his chest sent him reeling. He tried to clutch the edge of the table, dropped the revolver, staggered, and sat down on the floor, looking around him in astonishment. He didn't recognize his own room as he looked up from the floor at the bent legs of the table, the wastepaper basket, the tiger-skin rug. The hurried, creaking steps of his servant coming through the drawing-room brought him back to himself. He made an effort to think and realized that he was on the floor; and seeing blood on the tiger-skin rug and on his arm, he understood that he had shot himself.

"Idiotic! Missed!" he said, groping for the revolver. The revolver was right beside him — he was reaching farther off. Still feeling for it, he stretched out to the other side, and not having the strength to keep his balance, fell over, streaming with blood.

The elegant, whiskered manservant, who used to complain endlessly to his acquaintances about the delicacy of his nerves, was so panic-stricken at the sight of his master lying on the floor that he left him bleeding while he ran for help. An hour later Varya, his brother's wife, had arrived, and with the help of three doctors she had sent for in all directions, all of whom turned up at the same moment, she got the wounded man into bed and stayed to nurse him.
